content: The content provided appears to be a detailed and highly technical summary of various studies, interventions, and systematic reviews related to antenatal care, pregnancy management, and associated outcomes. 1. Screening for Intimate Partner Violence (IPV): A systematic review by Rogozinska et al. (2016) evaluated the accuracy of on-site tests for detecting asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy. The findings were based on studies with varying levels of bias and imprecision, with wide confidence intervals (CIs) and limited overlap in CIs across studies. 2. Fetal Movement Counting: Mangesi et al. (2015) compared routine daily fetal movement counting with usual practices for assessing fetal well-being. The evidence was of very low certainty due to high risk of bias, reliance on a single randomized controlled trial (RCT), and wide CIs despite a sample size exceeding 300 participants. 3. Robert Peter et al. The evidence was rated as low certainty due to reliance on a single RCT, wide CIs, and a low total event rate. 4. Antenatal Cardiotocography (CTG): Grivell et al. (2015) reviewed the use of routine antenatal CTG versus no routine CTG for fetal assessment. No direct evidence on the effects of this intervention was available. 5. Ultrasound Scans in Pregnancy: Early ultrasound scans (<24 weeks) were compared with selective or concealed scans. Whitworth et al. (2015) found low-certainty evidence due to moderate to high risk of bias and severe heterogeneity (I² > 60%). Late ultrasound scans (>24 weeks) were also evaluated, with similar limitations in evidence quality. 6. Doppler Ultrasound in Normal Pregnancy: Alfirevic et al. (2015) reviewed routine Doppler ultrasound of fetal blood vessels versus no Doppler. The evidence was moderate in quality but limited by high heterogeneity and wide CIs. Multiple Doppler ultrasounds were compared with no Doppler, with moderate-certainty evidence but significant bias in blinding and randomization procedures. Single Doppler ultrasound studies provided very low-certainty evidence due to reliance on a single RCT and wide CIs. 7. Antibiotics for Asymptomatic Bacteriuria (ASB): Smaill and Vazquez (2015) found low-certainty evidence for the use of antibiotics versus no treatment for ASB in pregnancy, with severe heterogeneity and small sample sizes contributing to the limitations. 8. Prophylactic Antibiotics for Recurrent Urinary Tract Infections (RUTI): Schneeberger et al. (2015) reported low-certainty evidence for preventing RUTI during pregnancy, with wide CIs and unexplained heterogeneity. 9. Antenatal Anti-D Immunoglobulin Prophylaxis: McBain et al. (2015) reviewed the use of anti-D immunoglobulin for preventing Rhesus alloimmunization. The evidence was of very low certainty due to small sample sizes and wide CIs. 10. Preventive Anthelmintic Treatment: Salam et al. (2015) evaluated anthelmintic administration during pregnancy. The evidence was moderate in quality but limited by unexplained heterogeneity and wide CIs. 11. Tetanus Toxoid Vaccination: Demicheli et al. (2015) reviewed tetanus toxoid vaccination for preventing neonatal tetanus. The evidence was moderate in quality but limited by small sample sizes and wide CIs. 12. Interventions for Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy: Most studies provided low-certainty evidence due to small sample sizes, wide CIs, and high risk of bias. 13. Interventions for Heartburn in Pregnancy: Phupong and Hanprasertpong (2015) reviewed pharmacological treatments versus placebo or lifestyle changes. The evidence was very low in certainty due to severe heterogeneity and small sample sizes. 14. Interventions for Leg Cramps: Zhou et al. (2015) evaluated oral magnesium, calcium, and vitamin B1/B6 supplementation. The evidence was low in certainty due to small sample sizes and wide CIs. 15. Interventions for Low Back and Pelvic Pain: Liddle and Pennick (2015) reviewed exercise, acupuncture, and multimodal interventions. The evidence was low to moderate in certainty, with limitations including small sample sizes and unexplained heterogeneity. 16. Interventions for Constipation in Pregnancy: Rungsiprakarn et al. (2015) reviewed fiber supplementation and laxatives. The evidence was very low in certainty due to small sample sizes and wide CIs. 17. Interventions for Varicose Veins and Edema: Smyth et al. (2015) evaluated treatments such as rutoside, pneumatic compression, reflexology, and water immersion. The evidence was low in certainty due to small sample sizes and wide CIs. 18. Woman-Held Case Notes: Brown et al. (2015) reviewed the impact of giving women their own case notes during pregnancy. The evidence was low in certainty due to unexplained data discrepancies and severe heterogeneity. 19. Midwife-Led Continuity of Care (MLCC): Sandall et al. (2015) compared MLCC with other care models. The evidence was low in certainty due to asymmetry in funnel plots and unexplained heterogeneity. 20. Group Antenatal Care (ANC): Catling et al. (2015) reviewed group ANC versus individual ANC. The evidence was low in certainty due to reliance on a single study and wide CIs. 21. Focused ANC (FANC) Model: Dowswell et al. (2015) compared the FANC model (minimum of four visits) with the standard ANC model (minimum of eight visits). The evidence was moderate in certainty but limited by unexplained heterogeneity. 22. Community-Based Interventions: Mbuagbaw et al. (2015) reviewed community-based interventions such as women’s groups and home visits. The evidence was moderate in certainty but limited by wide CIs and unexplained heterogeneity. 23. Search Strategies for ANC Guidelines: A systematic search conducted in December 2013 identified existing ANC guidelines from databases such as PubMed, LILACS, and TRIP. The search was broad and included guidelines published after January 2000.
